title: What does a 1% fee really cost?
hook: A 1% yearly fee sounds like 1% of your money. Thirty years says otherwise.

knows: that savings can grow by compounding (compound-interest lesson)
doesNotKnow: that a yearly percentage fee is taken from a growing balance, so its dollar cost grows too
that money taken by a fee also stops compounding

misconception: A 1% fee is just 1% of what I end up with.
objective: The learner can explain that a yearly fee is a rate that compounds against the saver, so over decades a 1-point lower return can cost about a quarter of the final balance.

claims.text: With a fixed yearly return, a balance after t years is deposit × (1 + rate)^t.
claims.source: Each year multiplies the balance by (1 + r). Standard future-value result, e.g. Brealey, Myers & Allen, Principles of Corporate Finance, ch. 2.

claims.text: $10,000 at 7% a year for 30 years grows to about $76,123.
Net of a 1% fee (6% a year), the same $10,000 grows to about $57,435 in 30 years.
The 1% fee costs about $18,688, about 24.5% of the no-fee balance.
The stage readouts for other fees use the same formula: net balance = 10,000 × (1.07 − fee)^30; e.g. a 0.5% fee costs about 13.1% and a 2% fee about 43.2% of the no-fee balance.
Money taken by a fee no longer earns a return, so the dollar gap widens fastest in the later years.
claims.source: The gap 10,000 × (1.07^t − 1.06^t) grows each year by 10,000 × (0.07 × 1.07^t − 0.06 × 1.06^t), which increases with t.

claims.text: The lesson is a model: a steady 7% gross return with the fee subtracted from it each year, no deposits, withdrawals or taxes. Real returns vary. It is not investment advice.
claims.source: Assumptions of the lesson's own calculation in Demo.tsx (the brief's net-6% convention; charging 1% of the balance after growth, 1.07 × 0.99, gives a slightly larger 26%).

recall.question: Two funds earn the same before fees. One charges 1% a year more. Over 30 years, the extra fee costs you about…
options: A quarter of the final balance
recall.why: A yearly fee is a rate taken from a growing balance, and what it takes stops compounding, so a 1-point gap grows to roughly a quarter of the outcome over 30 years at typical returns.
